questions.stem: Which of the following is capital expenditure?
options: Building a new hospital
Paying nurses' salaries
Paying a state pension
Buying medicines for a clinic
questions.why: Capital expenditure creates assets that last beyond the current period, and it raises aggregate supply as well as aggregate demand.
whyNot: Salaries are current expenditure.
A pension is a transfer payment.
Consumables are current expenditure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a transfer payment?
options: Unemployment benefit
A teacher's salary
A new railway line
School textbooks
questions.why: A transfer payment is made with no good or service received in return.
whyNot: That is current expenditure on a service.
That is capital expenditure.
That is current expenditure.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines crowding out?
options: The reduction in private sector activity caused by government borrowing raising interest rates
The increase in private investment caused by public investment
The displacement of imports by domestic production
The movement of workers from the public to the private sector
questions.why: It also occurs through the public sector absorbing resources the private sector would have used.
whyNot: That is crowding in.
That is import substitution.
That is a labour market shift.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the dependency ratio?
options: The ratio of the non-working population to the working population
The ratio of government spending to GDP
The ratio of benefits to wages
The ratio of imports to exports
questions.why: An ageing population raises it, which raises spending on pensions, health and social care.
whyNot: That is the size of the state.
That is a replacement rate.
That is a trade ratio.

questions.stem: Why does capital expenditure have a different long-run effect from a transfer payment?
options: Capital expenditure shifts aggregate supply to the right as well as aggregate demand
Transfer payments raise aggregate supply and capital expenditure does not
Transfer payments have no effect on aggregate demand
Neither affects aggregate demand
questions.why: Capital spending creates productive capacity, so the same sum has a very different long-run effect from spending on transfers.
whyNot: It is the other way round.
Recipients have a high marginal propensity to consume, so AD rises.
Both raise AD.

questions.stem: Why does public spending tend to rise as a share of GDP as economies develop?
options: Demand for health, education and transport is income elastic, so it rises more than proportionately
Public services become cheaper to provide
Tax rates automatically rise with income
Populations become younger as incomes rise
questions.why: Citizens of richer countries demand more and better public services, which is sometimes called Wagner's law.
whyNot: Public service costs tend to rise faster than average prices.
Rates are set by policy.
Populations typically age as incomes rise.

questions.stem: Why can the same demographic argument produce different spending patterns?
options: An ageing population raises pension and health spending, while a young one raises education spending
Demographics have no effect on spending composition
All populations age at the same rate
Age distribution affects only tax revenue
questions.why: So the answer depends on which stage of development the country in the source is at.
whyNot: Age structure directly drives the composition of spending.
Ageing rates differ substantially.
It affects both spending and revenue.

questions.stem: Under what condition is crowding out weakest?
options: In a deep recession with spare capacity and unemployed resources
When the economy is at full capacity
When private investment is highly interest sensitive
When the government borrows entirely from domestic banks
questions.why: Government spending then uses resources that would otherwise be idle, which is the central Keynesian point.
whyNot: Full capacity is when crowding out is strongest.
High interest sensitivity makes crowding out larger.
The source of borrowing matters, but capacity is the key condition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines crowding in?
options: Public investment raising the return on private investment, so private investment rises
Government borrowing raising interest rates
The private sector taking over public services
Workers moving into the public sector
questions.why: Naming it is a strong evaluative move, because it works in the opposite direction to crowding out.
whyNot: That is crowding out.
That is privatisation.
That is a labour market shift.

questions.stem: Why is it said that the composition of public spending matters more than its level?
options: Capital spending on infrastructure and education raises long-run capacity; poorly targeted subsidies do not
The level cannot be measured accurately
All public spending has identical effects
The level is determined internationally
questions.why: Countries with high spending and high productivity exist, and so do countries with high spending and low productivity.
whyNot: It is measured as a share of GDP routinely.
The effects differ sharply by type.
It is a national policy choice.

questions.stem: Why would a market fail to provide public goods such as law and defence?
options: Because of the free rider problem: people can consume them without paying
Because they are too cheap to be profitable
Because governments prohibit private provision
Because demand for them is very low
questions.why: No productive economy functions without them, which is why their provision is an argument for public spending regardless of its level.
whyNot: They are expensive, and the problem is non-excludability.
Some private provision exists; the problem is under-provision.
Demand is high; the problem is charging for it.

questions.stem: Why is borrowing to fund capital spending more defensible than borrowing for transfers?
options: The asset created is still there for future generations to use, so they receive the benefit with the cost
Capital spending is cheaper than transfers
Transfers cannot legally be funded by borrowing
Capital spending has no effect on the debt
questions.why: That distinction between borrowing to invest and borrowing to consume is the key point on intergenerational equity.
whyNot: Cost is not the argument.
Both can be funded by borrowing.
Both add to the debt.

questions.stem: Why do public service costs tend to rise faster than average prices?
options: They are labour-intensive and productivity growth in them is slow
Public sector workers are always paid more
Governments deliberately overpay suppliers
Public services are subject to higher indirect taxes
questions.why: This is the Baumol effect, and it means maintaining the same level of service requires rising spending over time.
whyNot: Relative pay varies and is not the mechanism.
Procurement problems exist but are not the general explanation.
Taxation of public services is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an argument that higher public spending reduces productivity growth?
options: Public sector productivity growth is generally slower, so a larger public sector lowers the average
Public spending never funds infrastructure
Public goods reduce private output
Education spending reduces human capital
questions.why: Higher taxation to fund it and the risk of government failure are the other arguments.
whyNot: Infrastructure is a major category of public capital spending.
Public goods are a precondition for private output.
It raises human capital.

questions.stem: Why is the boundary between current spending and investment in capacity less sharp than the classification implies?
options: Teachers' salaries are current expenditure and they produce human capital
Capital spending is always recorded as current spending
Transfers are classified as capital spending
The classification is chosen arbitrarily each year
questions.why: Making that point shows real understanding of what the classification does and does not capture.
whyNot: The two are recorded separately.
Transfers are a distinct third category.
The classification follows consistent definitions.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a free rider?
options: Someone who consumes a public good without paying for it
Someone who receives a transfer payment
Someone who uses public transport without a ticket
Someone who avoids paying income tax
questions.why: Non-excludability means the market cannot charge, which is why public goods must be publicly funded.
whyNot: Transfers are received under entitlement rules.
That is fare evasion from an excludable service.
That is tax evasion.
